name: Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Country-Year Dataset
version: v16 (Country-Year: V-Dem Full+Others; also Core, Country-Date and Coder-Level files)
maintainer: V-Dem Institute, Department of Political Science, University of Gothenburg (Sweden); PIs include Michael Coppedge, John Gerring, Carl Henrik Knutsen, Staffan I. Lindberg and Jan Teorell, with a large international team
secondary_domains: HIST; PARTY; ELEC; CONST; HR; TEXT; GENDER
unit_of_analysis: country-year (country-date and coder-level versions also released)
spatial_coverage: Global; 202 country units, including historical polities and some pre-independence colonies (V-Dem codebook v16, section 1.6)
temporal_coverage: 1789-2025 (contemporary coding 1900-2025; Historical V-Dem coding 1789-1920; many indices start in 1900)
temporal_resolution: annual (country-year); daily dates in the country-date file
size: Full+Others: 531 V-Dem indicators, 251 indices and 62 indicators from other sources; Core: 5 high-level indices, 93 sub-indices, 179 indicators; 202 country units; number of country-year rows UNVERIFIED
key_variables: v2x_polyarchy (electoral democracy index); v2x_libdem (liberal democracy index); v2x_partipdem (participatory democracy index); v2x_delibdem (deliberative democracy index); v2x_egaldem (egalitarian democracy index); v2x_regime (Regimes of the World); v2x_accountability, v2x_veracc, v2x_horacc, v2x_diagacc (accountability indices); v2x_liberal (liberal component); v2exl_legit* (legitimation strategies); country_id, COWcode
generation_method: expert coding (country-expert surveys, typically five or more experts per country-year) combined with research-assistant coding of factual (A-type) indicators and data imported from other sources
measurement_approach: Bayesian ordinal IRT measurement model (Pemstein et al.) turns expert ratings into latent scores with highest-posterior-density intervals; higher-order indices are built with Bayesian factor analysis and the multiplicative/additive formulas documented in the codebook
download_url: https://v-dem.net/data/the-v-dem-dataset/country-year-v-dem-fullothers-v16/ (web form asks for an email address and privacy-policy consent; no account); earlier versions at https://v-dem.net/data/dataset-archive/
formats: Stata; CSV; R; SPSS (coder-level file: CSV and R only)
programmatic_access: vdemdata R package (https://github.com/vdeminstitute/vdemdata; bundles V-Dem v16 Full+Others and V-Party; functions find_var, var_info, plot_indicator); democracyData R package (vdem objects); also redistributed in QoG Standard and Demscore; R package demcon 0.4.0 (DANTE Project / ISciences; get_vdem() download helper plus vignettes on V-Dem pre-processing and country-coding pitfalls when merging) was archived on CRAN on 2023-10-16 for policy violation; source and documentation remain on GitLab (dante-sttr/demcon, last activity 2023-09), so treat it as legacy
citation: Coppedge, Michael, John Gerring, Carl Henrik Knutsen, Staffan I. Lindberg, Jan Teorell, et al. 2026. "V-Dem Country-Year Dataset v16." Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Project. https://doi.org/10.23696/vdemds26. Reference article: Coppedge, Michael, John Gerring, David Altman, Michael Bernhard, Steven Fish, Allen Hicken, Matthew Kroenig, Staffan I. Lindberg, Kelly McMann, Pamela Paxton, Holli A. Semetko, Svend-Erik Skaaning, Jeffrey Staton, and Jan Teorell. 2011. "Conceptualizing and Measuring Democracy: A New Approach." Perspectives on Politics 9 (2): 247-267.
notable_uses: Lührmann and Lindberg 2019 (Democratization, third wave of autocratization); Claassen 2019 (APSR, thermostatic democratic support); Boese et al. 2021 (Democratization, democratic resilience)
merge_keys: V-Dem country_id; country_text_id; COWcode (COW code); year
related_datasets: REG-007; REG-009; Boix-Miller-Rosato; REG-018; REG-030; Global State of Democracy; REG-003; Historical V-Dem; REG-004; PARTY-005; INFRA-001
quality_justification: Validity 5: each index rests on an explicit conceptual model of five democracy principles, and the project's methods work tests the indices against Polity, Freedom House and other measures. Reliability 5: several experts rate each observation, Bayesian IRT adjusts for differing coder thresholds, uncertainty intervals are reported and coder-level data are released. Transparency 5: full codebook, methodology, aggregation-structure and country-unit documents, plus an appendix listing changes between versions. Coverage 5: 202 units, 1789/1900-2025, with gaps in country coding periods documented. Comparability 4: units and model are consistent, but each release re-estimates past scores (not comparable across versions), and the 1900-1920 overlap between historical and contemporary coding can create artificial breaks; both issues are documented. Maintenance 5: annual versioned releases since v5 (2016) with a public archive. Accessibility 5: free, four standard formats plus an R package; only an email web form. Adoption 5: the dominant democracy measure in top comparative and IR journals.
strengths: Disaggregated, multidimensional measurement (hundreds of indicators feeding five high-level democracy indices); explicit uncertainty estimates; very long time series; coder-level data and full documentation; regular releases and an R package.
limitations: Expert-coded evaluative indicators may carry time-varying coder bias: Little and Meng 2024 (PS: Political Science & Politics) argue expert indices overstate recent backsliding compared with objective indicators (replies include Knutsen et al. 2024 and Weitzel et al. 2024). Scores change retroactively across versions, so replication requires pinning a version. Indices are sensitive to aggregation formulas. Small countries with fewer than five coders have wider intervals. The historical/contemporary overlap (1900-1920) may contain artificial jumps.
best_used_for: Cross-national, long-run analysis of democracy and its components; studies that need measurement uncertainty; disaggregated institutional features (elections, judiciary, media, civil society).
avoid_for: Treating point estimates as exact or comparing values across dataset versions; claims that rest on objectively observable events alone without acknowledging the expert-judgment component.

citation: Knutsen, Carl Henrik, Jan Teorell, Tore Wig, Agnes Cornell, John Gerring, Haakon Gjerløw, Svend-Erik Skaaning, Daniel Ziblatt, Kyle L. Marquardt, Daniel Pemstein, and Brigitte Seim. 2019. "Introducing the Historical Varieties of Democracy Dataset: Political Institutions in the Long 19th Century." Journal of Peace Research 56 (3): 440-451.
notable_uses: Teorell et al. 2019 (Studies in Comparative International Development, measuring polyarchy 1900-2017); Brambor, Goenaga, Lindvall and Teorell 2020 (Comparative Political Studies, information capacity of the state); Coppedge et al. 2020 (Varieties of Democracy book, Cambridge UP)

quality_justification: Validity 4: uses V-Dem's explicit concepts and the JPR article reports validity checks, but rating 19th-century polities raises source-scarcity problems. Reliability 4: IRT model with uncertainty, but fewer experts per polity than contemporary V-Dem. Transparency 4: documented in V-Dem codebook Part IV and the article; the project page was last updated in 2022 and offers no standalone documentation. Coverage 4: up to 91 polities 1789-1920, fewer for some C-type variables. Comparability 3: the codebook warns of artificial breaks in the 1900-1920 overlap with contemporary coding and keeps separate v3 variables where codings disagree. Maintenance 3: no standalone versioned release; folded into annual V-Dem updates. Accessibility 4: free, but only available inside the large V-Dem file. Adoption 3: used mainly in historical-institutional and long-run democratization studies.

limitations: Sources are sparse for early periods; coverage of some C-type variables is still incomplete; overlap-period discrepancies with contemporary coding (the codebook warns of possible artificial jumps around 1900); no separate release, so version tracking depends on the V-Dem release.
best_used_for: Long-run analyses of democratization and state institutions in the 19th century; extending V-Dem time series before 1900.
avoid_for: Analyses that splice historical and contemporary series around 1900-1920 without checking the overlap-discrepancy variables.

name: Regimes of the World (RoW)
maintainer: Anna Lührmann, Marcus Tannenberg and Staffan I. Lindberg; V-Dem Institute, University of Gothenburg (v16 codebook project managers: Marcus Tannenberg and Staffan I. Lindberg; Valeriya Mechkova also for v2x_regime_amb)
temporal_coverage: 1900-2025 (V-Dem v16 codebook); 1900-2016 in the 2018 reference article
size: 2 variables (a 4-category version and a 10-category version with ambiguous cases) within the V-Dem country-year data
key_variables: v2x_regime (0 closed autocracy, 1 electoral autocracy, 2 electoral democracy, 3 liberal democracy); v2x_regime_amb (with upper/lower ambiguous categories); inputs: v2x_polyarchy; v2x_liberal; v2elmulpar_osp; v2elfrfair_osp; v2cltrnslw_osp; v2clacjstm_osp; v2clacjstw_osp
generation_method: aggregation of V-Dem expert-coded and factual indicators
measurement_approach: Rule-based categorical classification using thresholds on V-Dem indices and indicators (e.g., EDI above 0.5, liberal component above 0.8); ambiguous cases identified from Bayesian highest-posterior-density intervals
download_url: Included in the V-Dem Country-Year (Full+Others and Core) files: https://v-dem.net/data/the-v-dem-dataset/
formats: Stata; CSV; R; SPSS (via V-Dem files)
license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (V-Dem dataset); reference article CC BY 4.0
programmatic_access: vdemdata R package (variable v2x_regime in the vdem object)
citation: Lührmann, Anna, Marcus Tannenberg, and Staffan I. Lindberg. 2018. "Regimes of the World (RoW): Opening New Avenues for the Comparative Study of Political Regimes." Politics and Governance 6 (1): 60-77.
notable_uses: Lührmann and Lindberg 2019 (Democratization); Haggard and Kaufman 2021 (Backsliding, Cambridge UP); Claassen 2019 (APSR)
related_datasets: REG-001; Cheibub-Gandhi-Vreeland Democracy-Dictatorship; Boix-Miller-Rosato; Geddes-Wright-Frantz Autocratic Regimes; REG-004; REG-009
quality_justification: Validity 4: explicit four-category typology tied to Dahl's polyarchy plus liberal principles; the article compares it with other regime datasets (they disagree on 7-12% of country-years), but the thresholds are stipulated. Reliability 4: inherits V-Dem IRT uncertainty and flags ambiguous cases in v2x_regime_amb. Transparency 5: aggregation rules and source variables are spelled out in codebook section 5.1. Coverage 4: global, but starts in 1900 although the underlying EDI goes back to 1789. Comparability 4: consistent rules, but categories can shift between V-Dem releases as inputs are re-estimated. Maintenance 5: updated in every V-Dem release (data release 9-16 per codebook). Accessibility 5: free in all V-Dem formats and the R package. Adoption 5: widely used regime typology (V-Dem Democracy Reports, top journals).
strengths: Simple, interpretable typology that separates electoral from closed autocracies; built on V-Dem's detailed indicators; the ambiguity version carries measurement uncertainty forward; updated annually.
limitations: Thresholds (e.g., EDI 0.5) are analyst choices, so cases near the cut-offs can flip between versions; categories inherit any bias in V-Dem expert ratings (see Little and Meng 2024 on expert-coded indices); years before 1900 are not classified.
best_used_for: Descriptive regime classification, regime-type controls and transitions between autocracy and democracy since 1900.
avoid_for: Fine-grained variation within categories (use the continuous V-Dem indices) and analyses before 1900.
found_via: GUPEA repository (University of Gothenburg); Politics and Governance reference article; vdemdata R package; V-Dem codebook
institutional_access_note: Free as part of V-Dem; reference article is open access.
unverified_notes: Temporal coverage differs: the article covers 1900-2016; the V-Dem v16 codebook lists 1900-2025. No standalone RoW landing page exists; landing_url is the V-Dem dataset page. The most-cited version (2018 article, based on an early V-Dem release) differs from current v16 values. OpenAlex cited_by_count 614 (checked 2026-11). name: Freedom in the World
version: Freedom in the World 2026 (covers events of calendar 2025); public historical files: Country and Territory Ratings and Statuses 1973-2024; Aggregate Category and Subcategory Scores 2003-2024
maintainer: Freedom House, Washington, DC (research team with external country analysts and expert advisers)
spatial_coverage: Global: 195 countries and 13 related or disputed territories (2026 edition)
temporal_coverage: 1972-2025 (statuses and 1-7 ratings from the 1973 edition; total PR/CL scores from 2003; subcategory A-G scores from 2006; all 25 indicators from 2013)
size: 208 countries and territories per edition; N obs UNVERIFIED
key_variables: status (Free/Partly Free/Not Free); political rights rating (1-7); civil liberties rating (1-7); political rights score (0-40); civil liberties score (0-60); total score (0-100); subcategory scores A-G; indicator scores (25 indicators); electoral democracy designation
measurement_approach: Additive index: 10 political-rights and 15 civil-liberties indicators each scored 0-4 by country analysts, reviewed in regional meetings; scores sum to 0-100 and are converted into 1-7 ratings and a three-category status.
download_url: https://freedomhouse.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/Country_and_Territory_Ratings_and_Statuses_FIW_1973-2024.xlsx; https://freedomhouse.org/sites/default/files/2024-02/Aggregate_Category_and_Subcategory_Scores_FIW_2003-2024.xlsx; newer and indicator-level data via https://freedomhouse.org/data-request
formats: Excel (.xlsx); PDF report and methodology; country narratives (HTML)
license: Free for personal, academic and nonprofit use; commercial use needs written permission from Freedom House
programmatic_access: democracyData R package (fh, fh_full, fh_electoral; updated to the FIW 2026 workbook); QoG Standard dataset (fh_ variables); Our World in Data
citation: Freedom House. 2026. Freedom in the World 2026. Washington, DC: Freedom House. https://freedomhouse.org/report/freedom-world
notable_uses: Barro 1999 (Determinants of Democracy); Acemoglu et al. 2008 (Income and Democracy, American Economic Review)
merge_keys: Country name only (no numeric codes in FH files); democracyData and QoG add COW/Gleditsch-Ward/ISO codes
related_datasets: REG-011; REG-010; TEXT-064; REG-007; REG-001; REG-053; Global State of Democracy
quality_justification: Validity 3: explicit checklist of political rights and civil liberties, but the index blends regime institutions with rights outcomes and has faced documented bias critiques. Reliability 3: analysts must anchor score changes in events, and scores are reviewed in regional meetings and cross-checked by staff and 28 expert advisers; no inter-coder statistics or uncertainty estimates. Transparency 3: annual methodology and full checklist published, country narratives explain scores, but indicator-level scores are public only from 2013 and sources are not itemised. Coverage 4: every country plus selected territories since the early 1970s, though detailed scores begin only in 2003/2006/2013. Comparability 3: methodology revised over time, 1-7 ratings dropped from reports in 2020, region assignments changed in 2022. Maintenance 5: uninterrupted annual editions. Accessibility 3: historical Excel files are open, but the current edition and indicator data require a request form. Adoption 5: one of the two most-used democracy measures in top journals.
strengths: Current to the most recent year with a long annual track record; includes territories; separates political rights from civil liberties; narrative reports justify each score.
limitations: Scores mix regime type with rights performance, so outcomes such as repression enter the measure. Bollen and Paxton (2000, Comparative Political Studies) document rater-specific measurement error in subjective democracy ratings including Freedom House. Steiner (2016, Journal of Comparative Policy Analysis) finds evidence of political bias favouring US allies, smaller in later years. Högström (2013, Government and Opposition) shows Freedom House and Polity IV yield different results. Fine-grained scores are unavailable before 2003; latest data no longer freely downloadable.
best_used_for: Up-to-date cross-national comparisons of political rights and civil liberties; broad regime classification (Free/Partly Free/Not Free); studies needing territories as well as states.
avoid_for: Studies that treat civil liberties or repression as outcomes of democracy (risk of circularity); long time series of continuous scores before 2003; designs sensitive to possible geopolitical rating bias.

name: Boix-Miller-Rosato Dichotomous Coding of Democracy
maintainer: Carles Boix (Princeton University), Michael K. Miller (George Washington University; contact), Sebastian Rosato (University of Notre Dame)
spatial_coverage: Global: all sovereign countries including micro-states (222 countries); UN membership generally used to date micro-state entry
size: 19,130 country-year democracy observations; 222 countries; 11 variables (codebook v4.0)
key_variables: democracy; democracy_omitteddata; democracy_femalesuffrage; democracy_trans; democracy_breakdowns; democracy_duration; ccode; abbreviation
generation_method: expert coding (author coding from historical sources)
measurement_approach: dichotomous coding: democracy requires both contestation (free and fair elections choosing leaders) and participation (suffrage threshold); variant adds a female-suffrage requirement
formats: tab-delimited (from Stata .dta and CSV), plain text; author page also offers Stata, Excel and R files
programmatic_access: democracyData R package (bmr; GitHub only); QoG Standard dataset (bmr_ variables); Harvard Dataverse API
citation: Boix, Carles, Michael Miller, and Sebastian Rosato. 2013. "A Complete Data Set of Political Regimes, 1800-2007." Comparative Political Studies 46 (12): 1523-54.
notable_uses: Acemoglu et al. 2019; Lührmann, Tannenberg and Lindberg 2018; Przeworski 2019
merge_keys: COW code (ccode); ISO3 / World Bank 3-letter code; UCDP 3-letter code
related_datasets: CGV; REG-017; REG-018; REG-007; V-Dem RoW; Anckar-Fredriksson Political Regimes of the World
quality_justification: Validity 4: explicit minimalist concept (contestation plus participation) with a stated suffrage threshold and a female-suffrage variant; no formal validation statistics seen. Reliability 3: rules and coding sources are in the 2013 article, but no intercoder or uncertainty figures. Transparency 4: two-page codebook with full variable list and a dated change log for v1.0-v4.0; case-level justifications are only in the article. Coverage 5: 222 countries 1800-2020 including micro-states, with explicit treatment of occupation and state collapse (democracy_omitteddata). Comparability 4: same rules across time; version changes are listed case by case. Maintenance 3: four versions over nine years; latest data end in 2020. Accessibility 5: CC0 on Harvard Dataverse with DOI, multiple formats, R package and QoG. Adoption 5: reference article has about 1,080 OpenAlex citations including APSR/JPE-level work.
strengths: Longest-running global dichotomous democracy series; minimal, transparent decision rule; documented version changes; female-suffrage variant; CC0 with persistent DOI.
limitations: Binary coding discards variation within democracies and autocracies; ends in 2020; no measurement-uncertainty or intercoder statistics; earlier versions (v2.0/v3.0 to 2015) remain widely cited and differ in several transition dates. No published methodological critique was located in this check.
best_used_for: Long-run (19th-century onward) analyses of democratic transitions and breakdowns; survival models; robustness checks against Polity or V-Dem.
avoid_for: Measuring degrees of democracy or backsliding within regime types; years after 2020.
found_via: Guide: Princeton University (https://libguides.princeton.edu/politics/indicators); Guide: University of Essex (https://library.essex.ac.uk/politics/dem); PolData; democracyData R package; QoG Data Finder; Harvard Dataverse; Our World in Data
institutional_access_note: Free and open (CC0); no subscription needed.
unverified_notes: citation_count: Google Scholar blocked (robot check); OpenAlex cited_by_count 1082 for the 2013 article (checked 2026-11). Version note: democracyData README lists bmr as 'Version 4.0, 1800-2015' but the v4.0 codebook and Dataverse record say 1800-2020; the 1800-2015 release is the separate v3.0 Dataverse record (doi 10.7910/DVN/FJLMKT, OpenAlex). The 2013 article (v1.0, 1800-2007, 219 countries) is the most cited version and differs from v4.0 (e.g., France, Chile, Cyprus, Panama, Sri Lanka, Uruguay transition dates changed in v4.0). name: Polity5: Political Regime Characteristics and Transitions
version: Polity5 dataset version 2018 (files p5v2018 annual and p5v2018d polity-case; users' manual dated 2020-04-23). Earlier versions in the same series: Polity I (Gurr, collected mid-1970s), Polity II (Gurr, Jaggers & Moore; ICPSR 9263), Polity III / Polity98 (data to 1998; ICPSR 6695), Polity IIId (PRIO dating revision, 1994-2000), Polity IV (2000 onward, annual updates to 2018, POLITY2 added 2002). Polity5 is a hybrid: Polity5-refined codes for 76 of 167 countries (flag P5), Polity IV values elsewhere and for 1800-1945.
maintainer: Monty G. Marshall (PI), Center for Systemic Peace and Societal-Systems Research Inc; Ted Robert Gurr (founder, University of Maryland)
spatial_coverage: Independent states with population above 500,000 in 2018 (167 countries in 2018)
temporal_resolution: annual (country-year file); daily-dated regime spells (case file)
size: 167 countries; N obs UNVERIFIED; manual documents 39 variables across the annual and case files
key_variables: polity; polity2; democ; autoc; durable; xrreg; xrcomp; xropen; xconst; parreg; parcomp; regtrans
measurement_approach: Additive index: democracy (0-10) minus autocracy (0-10) gives a 21-point polity score (-10 to +10) from six ordinal authority components; special codes -66/-77/-88 for interruption, interregnum and transition; polity2 converts these for time-series use (interregnum set to 0, transitions prorated).
formats: SPSS (.sav); Excel (.xls); PDF manual; Excel change log
license: No open licence stated; free download, INSCR page requires proper citation in published work; 'Polity' is a registered trademark of CSP

quality_justification: Validity 4: explicit authority-pattern concept with defined components, extensively benchmarked against Freedom House, V-Dem and dichotomous measures, though critiques show the composite is dominated by executive constraints. Reliability 3: manual reports Polity IV inter-coder tests (1999 target year: 74 of 148 cases identical, about 88% within two points) but no measurement uncertainty. Transparency 4: long users' manual with coding rules, annual change logs and Polity5 country narratives; country-level sources not itemised. Coverage 4: 1800-2018 for all states above 500,000 people; small states excluded and data stop in 2018. Comparability 3: hybrid release mixes Polity5-revised and Polity IV codes, the annual and case files use different transition standards, and polity2 interpolation creates artificial values. Maintenance 2: PITF funding ended in early 2020 and no data after 2018 have been released. Accessibility 4: open SPSS/Excel files and R/QoG redistribution, no API. Adoption 5: among the most-used regime measures in top journals.
strengths: Longest annual regime series with component-level detail; separates executive recruitment, executive constraints and political competition; case-format file dates regime changes; huge comparative literature makes results easy to benchmark.
limitations: Frozen at 2018 and only partly revised to Polity5 standards. Gleditsch and Ward (1997, JCR) show the democracy score mostly tracks executive constraints and that its categorical structure is often ignored. Vreeland (2008, JCR) shows the anocracy middle range partly codes political violence (parcomp/parreg factionalism), biasing civil-war studies. Plümper and Neumayer (2010, Political Analysis) argue polity2 values for interregnum/transition years lack face validity. Högström (2013, Government and Opposition) finds Polity IV and Freedom House are not interchangeable. The manual itself notes no inter-coder tests before 2000 and thin sources for small 19th-century states.
best_used_for: Long-run cross-national analysis of institutional regime type, especially executive constraints and recruitment; dating regime transitions; replication of the large Polity-based literature.
avoid_for: Post-2018 analysis; studies of civil conflict using the anocracy middle range without dropping violence-related components; fine-grained democratic quality among established democracies (ceiling at +10); micro-states.

quality_justification: Validity 3: criteria are explicitly defined with level descriptions, but they mix policies and institutions and embed a particular development-policy paradigm; IEG's evaluation found ratings correlate with similar indicators (more so for IBRD than IDA countries). Reliability 2: staff judgments with a two-stage regional and Bank-wide review for consistency, but no intercoder reliability or uncertainty estimates, and the written rationales and sub-ratings are confidential. Transparency 3: criteria document, process and weighting are public, but justifications and sub-scores are not. Coverage 2: only IDA-eligible countries (about 75-80) and only from 2005. Comparability 3: criteria revised in 2004, 2011 and 2016 (with the shift to triennial full assessments), documented in the criteria document; IDA membership changes alter the sample. Maintenance 4: annual releases with versioned catalog entries. Accessibility 5: CC BY, bulk CSV/Excel, API and R packages. Adoption 3: used mostly in aid-allocation, development and conflict research rather than core political science journals.
strengths: Fine-grained ratings of public-sector management, governance and policy for low-income countries from staff with in-country knowledge; consistent rating scale with explicit criteria; free and easy to access through World Bank APIs.
limitations: Covers only IDA-eligible countries, so samples are non-random and shift as countries graduate; ratings are internal World Bank staff judgments that directly determine IDA allocations, raising concerns about incentives and independence; a G-24 policy brief (2024) criticizes the lack of a government role or appeal process; the Independent Evaluation Group's evaluation (2009/2010) found weaker correlations with comparable indicators for IDA than IBRD countries; criteria revisions and the move to triennial full assessments (2016) affect over-time comparability; rationales are confidential.
best_used_for: Studies of aid allocation and conditionality, governance and public financial management in low-income countries, and as a comparison measure for governance in IDA countries.
avoid_for: Global or middle-/high-income country comparisons; pre-2005 analysis; treating scores as independent of World Bank lending decisions; fine year-to-year change in years with light updates.
